before.exam_tip_html: Examiners reward located detail. When you write about UK landscapes, name the place (Lake District, Norfolk Broads, Tarn Hows), give a specific number where you can (3,000 mm rainfall, 750,000 visitors), and link the human and physical sides together. For 6-mark ‘Explain with example’ questions, choose ONE landscape and develop it in depth rather than listing several superficially. For 8-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions on management, weigh up benefits against costs and reach a clear judgement at the end.
before.content_html:
Why UK Landscapes Look So Different

Travel from the Cairngorms to the Norfolk Broads and the land changes character every hour. The UK is small, but its landscapes are unusually varied because the rocks beneath them, the climate above them and the people who live on them are all different. Geographers describe these areas as distinctive landscapes — places that look and feel one way and not another.

A simple way to organise UK landscapes is the divide between upland and lowland regions. Uplands such as the Lake District, Snowdonia and the Scottish Highlands sit on hard, ancient rocks like granite and slate. Lowlands such as East Anglia and the Thames Basin sit on softer, younger rocks like chalk and clay. The boundary is sometimes called the Tees-Exe line because it runs roughly from the mouth of the Tees in the north-east to the mouth of the Exe in the south-west.

Key Fact

UK landscapes vary because of three combined factors: geology (hard upland rocks vs softer lowland rocks), climate (wetter, cooler in the north and west) and human activity (farming, settlement and tourism shape every area).

Upland Landscapes — The Lake District

The Lake District in north-west England is a classic upland landscape. Volcanic and slate rocks form steep mountains over 900 metres high. Glaciers carved deep U-shaped valleys, ribbon lakes such as Windermere, and sharp ridges. The climate is wet — over 3,000 mm of rain a year on the highest fells — so soils are thin and acidic. Farming is mostly sheep on the slopes and small dairy herds in the valleys. Stone walls, slate roofs and Herdwick sheep give the region its identity.

The Norfolk Broads are flat, low-lying wetlands in eastern England. Soft chalk and clay underlie the area, and rivers wind slowly across deep, fertile soils. Drier air from the continent means rainfall is only around 600 mm a year, so cereals and root crops thrive. The Broads themselves are flooded medieval peat pits, now a network of waterways used for sailing, birdwatching and reedbed conservation. The combination of agriculture, navigable water and gentle relief makes this a sharply different landscape from the Lake District — despite being on the same island.

How Human Activity Reshapes Landscapes

Even "natural" UK landscapes are shaped by people. Forests have been cleared for farming, moorland is burned for grouse, valleys are dammed for reservoirs, and stone walls divide every fell. Tourism is one of the strongest modern pressures. Honeypot sites pull crowds into a few small areas while quieter parts of the same region see almost nobody.

A honey pot site can be positive: visitor money supports cafes, hotels, mountain rescue teams and farm shops. Local people stay employed and young families do not all have to move away for work. Footpaths get repaired with tourist grants, and information signs help educate visitors about the environment.

However, the negative impacts are clear at busy weekends. Tarn Hows in the Lake District attracts more than 750,000 visitors a year. Footpaths erode into wide muddy scars, soil compacts so plants struggle to grow back, litter blows into streams, and verges get churned to mud by parked cars. House prices rise as second-home owners outbid local first-time buyers, and shops increasingly sell tourist gifts rather than everyday goods.

Key Fact

Every landscape has a carrying capacity — the number of visitors it can support before damage begins. Once exceeded, footpaths erode, vegetation dies and wildlife retreats. Managers use zoning, path repair and visitor caps to keep numbers within this limit.

Changing Rural Economies and Societies

UK uplands used to depend on farming, mining and forestry. Today, most upland incomes come from tourism, holiday lets and small service businesses. Some farmers diversify into glamping, farm shops or paying for visitors to walk on their land. Others sell up entirely. The result is a slow shift in identity: from working landscapes that produced wool and milk to leisure landscapes that produce experiences. Lowland villages have changed too — many now serve as commuter homes for nearby cities rather than farming hamlets.

Managing the Pressure

National park authorities lead most landscape management in the UK. The Lake District National Park, designated in 1951 and made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017, uses a mix of practical and policy tools.

Footpath repair. Fix the Fells, a partnership between the National Trust and the National Park, has restored hundreds of kilometres of mountain path using locally quarried stone since 2001. Stone pitching slows erosion and channels walkers along a single line.

Visitor management. Park-and-ride buses serve Honister and Buttermere on busy days, parking charges discourage dropping the car anywhere, and signs guide walkers to less crowded fells. This spreads the carrying capacity across more places.

Planning controls. Strict rules limit new building in the open fells, and second-home conversions are restricted in some valleys. The aim is to keep working communities alive, not just empty holiday cottages.

Distinctive UK landscapes are an inheritance from rocks, weather and centuries of human work. Keeping them distinctive needs active management — otherwise the very visitors who come to enjoy them will rub them away.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a honey pot site?
A) An area with no tourists at all
B) A small popular site that attracts large numbers of visitors
C) An entirely artificial landscape
D) A protected area where visitors are banned
practice_questions.marks: B) A small popular site that attracts large numbers of visitors [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two physical features that make UK upland landscapes distinctive.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hard, ancient rocks such as granite or slate that resist erosion and form steep relief.
• Higher rainfall (often over 2,000 mm a year) producing thin, acidic soils and fast-flowing streams.
• Glacial features such as U-shaped valleys, corries or ribbon lakes.
• Steep slopes and high altitudes (over 200–900 m).
[2 marks — 1 mark per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity has changed one UK landscape you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Lake District example. Students may include:
• Tourism has caused footpath erosion at sites such as Tarn Hows because thousands of walkers compress soil and kill vegetation.
• Second-home buying has pushed up house prices in villages such as Hawkshead, forcing young locals to move away.
• Farming has shaped the open fells through sheep grazing, which prevents trees regenerating.
[3 marks — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for a developed point linked to a named place. Mark scheme: Mastering — sustained explanation with named detail. Secure — clear cause-effect with a place name. Developing — basic point with limited place reference. Emerging — generic point.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the physical characteristics of one upland and one lowland UK landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Geology: the Lake District is built on hard volcanic rocks and slate, whereas the Norfolk Broads sit on soft chalk and clay.
• Relief: the Lake District is steep with peaks over 900 m, in contrast to the Broads which lie at or near sea level.
• Climate: rainfall in the Lake District exceeds 3,000 mm a year, whereas the Broads receive around 600 mm.
• Soils and farming: thin acidic soils in the uplands support sheep, whereas deep fertile soils in the Broads support cereals and reedbeds.
[4 marks — credit explicit comparison using words such as ‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’ or ‘similarly’. 1 mark per developed comparison.]

practice_questions.text: Using a named example, explain how visitor pressure can damage a UK landscape.
practice_questions.marks:
Tarn Hows in the Lake District is suitable. Students may include:
• Tarn Hows attracts over 750,000 visitors a year, well above its quiet carrying capacity.
• Heavy footfall compacts soil along paths, killing grass and mosses; rain then washes loose soil away creating wide muddy scars on the fellside.
• Cars overflow car parks and verges turn to mud, while litter blows into the tarn affecting wildlife.
• Honeypot pressure inflates house prices in nearby Hawkshead, pricing out local first-time buyers.
• Local shops shift towards tourist gifts and away from everyday goods, reducing services for residents.

Mastering: developed explanation with multiple linked impacts and accurate located detail.
Secure: clear explanation with a named site and at least two impacts.
Developing: some impacts identified but place detail thin.
Emerging: generic comments on tourism damage with no named example.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Tourism does more harm than good in UK upland landscapes.’
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and to oppose the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Footpath erosion at sites like Tarn Hows damages vegetation, soils and the visual landscape.
• Traffic congestion and air pollution accumulate on busy weekends, harming residents and wildlife.
• Second-home buying pushes house prices beyond local wages, hollowing out year-round communities.
• Honeypot pressure can overwhelm a single site’s carrying capacity in summer.

Arguments against:
• Tourism supports thousands of jobs in cafes, hotels, mountain rescue, transport and farm diversification.
• Visitor money funds path repair (Fix the Fells), ranger services and education programmes.
• National park designation, which protects the landscape, depends on tourism’s economic case.
• Visitor management strategies (park-and-ride, signage, zoning) can keep most pressure within carrying capacity.

Judgement: a balanced answer should weigh the cumulative damage at honeypot sites against the wider economic and protective benefits, ideally arguing that tourism is sustainable when managed but harmful when unmanaged.

Mastering: sustained evaluation with examples and a clear, supported conclusion.
Secure: clear arguments on both sides with named detail and a conclusion.
Developing: some arguments identified but conclusion weak or missing.
Emerging: simple list of points with no judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: Eduqas examiners often ask you to explain how a single landform forms. Use a clear sequence: name the process, say what it does to the rock, and link to the resulting feature. For 6-mark ‘Explain with example’ questions, name a specific UK river (Tees, Severn, Wye) and a specific feature on it (High Force waterfall, Severn meanders) rather than ‘a river in the UK’. Avoid mixing up weathering (in place) with erosion (transport) — this is a recurring error highlighted by markers.
before.content_html:
From Source to Mouth

A river starts in upland country as a thin trickle and ends at the coast as a wide, slow channel. Along the way it carves valleys, rolls boulders, sorts sand and dumps silt. Geographers split this work into three jobs: erosion, transport, and deposition. Different processes dominate in different parts of the river’s course, and that is why the landforms change as you move downstream.

Key Fact

Rivers erode in four ways: abrasion (load scrapes the bed), attrition (stones knock together and round off), hydraulic action (water force compresses air in cracks) and solution (slightly acidic water dissolves rock).

Upper Course — Cutting Down

In the uplands the river is small but steep. Most of its energy is used cutting downwards, called vertical erosion. Hydraulic action and abrasion grind a narrow slot into the rock. Weathering on the valley sides loosens material that mass movement carries down to the river. The result is a steep-sided, narrow V-shaped valley. Examples include the upper River Tees in the North Pennines and the head of the Wye in mid-Wales.

Waterfalls form when a river crosses a layer of hard rock that lies on top of softer rock. The softer rock erodes faster, leaving the harder rock as a lip. Plunge pools form below as falling water drills into the softer layer through hydraulic action and abrasion. Over centuries the lip is undercut and collapses, so the waterfall retreats upstream. The narrow steep-sided valley left behind is called a gorge. High Force on the River Tees has retreated to leave a gorge over a kilometre long.

Middle Course — Bending Sideways

As gradient slackens, the river begins to use its energy sideways rather than downwards. This is called lateral erosion. Slight bends become exaggerated as faster water on the outside of each curve scours the bank away while slow water on the inside drops sediment. The river develops a string of meanders.

Each meander has a deep, fast outer channel cut into a river cliff, and a shallow, slow inner channel where a slip-off slope of sand and gravel builds up. Over time meanders migrate sideways and downstream, carving a wide, flat valley floor.

Key Fact

On a meander, the strongest flow swings to the outside of the bend, eroding a steep river cliff. On the inside, slow water drops material as a slip-off slope of sand and gravel.

Lower Course — Spreading Out

By the lower course the river is wide, slow and heavy with load. It often flows across a broad floodplain built up over thousands of years. When the river overtops its banks, water slows, drops its coarsest sand close to the channel and carries fine silt across the field beyond. Repeated floods raise low ridges of sediment alongside the channel called levees, while the floodplain itself becomes a thick layer of fertile alluvium.

As meanders grow, the necks between two bends get narrower and narrower. A flood eventually slices through the neck, leaving the old loop cut off as an oxbow lake. Sediment seals the ends and the oxbow gradually fills in to become a marshy crescent in the field. The River Severn near Shrewsbury and the lower Trent are dotted with old oxbows.

Transporting the Load

Whatever the course, every river carries material. There are four ways. Traction rolls heavy boulders along the bed. Saltation bounces pebbles in short hops. Suspension lifts fine clay and silt to give the water its brown colour. Solution dissolves chemicals such as calcium carbonate. The mix changes downstream: traction dominates upland streams; suspension dominates lowland rivers like the Trent.

Why Energy Controls Everything

A river only does work when it has energy. Energy comes from gradient (slope) and discharge (volume per second). High in the hills the slope is steep, so even a small flow has enough energy to roll boulders and grind potholes. In the lowlands the slope is gentle, so most of the energy is needed just to keep the water moving, and the river starts to drop its load. After heavy rainfall, discharge spikes and even a sluggish lowland river can briefly carry boulders. The relationship between energy and load explains why the same river can erode in winter and deposit in summer.

Erosion, transport and deposition do not happen separately — they pass material along like a relay. A boulder loosened in the upper course is broken into pebbles by attrition in the middle, suspended as silt in the lower, and finally dropped on the floodplain or carried out to sea. The landforms (V-shaped valley, meander, oxbow, floodplain) are simply the visible record of this continuous, energy-driven journey from upland source to coastal mouth.

before.exam_tip_html: Eduqas markers reward answers that link the three factors rather than listing them. For 6-mark explanation questions, choose ONE place (Holderness, Lulworth, the Tees) and explain how geology, climate and human activity work together there. Mention specific named locations such as Mappleton or High Force, and include a number where you can (around 2 metres a year, fetch over 5,000 km). Avoid generic statements like ‘soft rock erodes faster’ without saying which rock and where.
before.content_html:
Why Some Landforms Change Faster

Two stretches of UK coast can sit only a short drive apart and erode at completely different rates. The Holderness coast in East Yorkshire is losing nearly two metres of cliff a year, while the chalk cliffs of the Seven Sisters lose only a few centimetres. The pattern is not random — three factors decide how fast a river or coastal landform changes: geology, climate and human activity.

Geology — Rock Type and Structure

The kind of rock at the surface decides how easily waves and rivers can break it down. Hard, well-cemented rocks like granite or chalk resist erosion. Soft, weakly-cemented rocks like clay and sand are stripped away quickly. The arrangement of these rocks matters too.

Key Fact

A concordant coastline has rock bands running parallel to the sea, so a single rock type forms long stretches of cliff. A discordant coastline has rock bands running at right angles to the sea, so soft rocks erode into bays between hard headlands.

A concordant coast looks regular and straight. The Lulworth coast in Dorset is partly concordant, with hard Portland limestone protecting softer rocks behind. A discordant coast looks crinkly. Studland Bay further east in Dorset shows it: hard chalk forms the headland at Old Harry Rocks while softer clays form Studland Bay just to the north. Geology also affects rivers — a waterfall like High Force on the Tees only exists because hard Whin Sill dolerite sits above softer limestone.

Climate — Wind, Waves and Storms

Climate sets the energy environment. The prevailing south-westerly wind drives most large UK waves onto the south and west coasts of Cornwall, Devon and west Wales. The further the wind has blown over open sea, the more powerful the waves — this distance is called fetch. Cornish beaches face an Atlantic fetch of over 5,000 km, so even a modest gale produces waves that pound the cliffs.

Most UK landform change happens in short, dramatic bursts during extreme weather. The winter of 2013–14 was one of the stormiest on record. Storms tore down the railway sea wall at Dawlish in Devon, the chalk cliff at Birling Gap in East Sussex lost up to seven years' worth of erosion in a single weekend, and rivers like the Thames and Severn flooded for weeks. Climate change is expected to bring more frequent storms and higher sea levels, accelerating both river and coastal erosion.

River discharge is also climate-driven. Heavy rain over saturated upland catchments — common in winter — produces sharp peaks in flow. These short, intense events do most of the erosion. In summer, low river levels mean little material moves and deposition can briefly dominate even in upper-course rivers.

Human Activity — Speeding Up and Slowing Down

Humans both protect and disturb landforms. Defences such as sea walls, groynes and rock armour are designed to slow erosion. They often work locally, but they can speed up erosion further along the coast.

A clear example is Mappleton on the Holderness coast. In 1991, two large rock groynes were built to trap sand on the village beach. The groynes worked — the village stopped collapsing into the sea — but they cut off the supply of sand moving south along the coast. Within a few years, cliffs at Cowden and Aldbrough just to the south began retreating much faster than before, leaving farms and roads at risk. The groynes saved one place by accelerating loss elsewhere.

Key Fact

Coastal defences interrupt the natural longshore drift, a process called terminal groyne syndrome. Sediment is trapped behind the structure, and the next stretch of coast is starved of sand — so it erodes faster.

Rivers Feel Human Pressure Too

River landforms also speed up or slow down because of what people do. Removing trees from upland catchments allows rain to reach rivers faster, sharpening flood peaks. Straightening river channels (channelisation) makes water flow more quickly, so erosion accelerates downstream. Dams and reservoirs do the opposite — they trap sediment and starve floodplains of new alluvium. The lower River Severn, controlled by reservoirs in mid-Wales, deposits less than it did a century ago.

Holderness illustrates all three factors at once. Geologically, the cliffs are made of soft boulder clay left behind by the last ice age — weak material that crumbles easily. Climatically, the coast faces a 700 km North Sea fetch and a stormy wind from the north-east. Socially, defences at Hornsea and Mappleton trap sand and starve the cliffs further south. Together these explain why the coast loses around two metres a year — one of the fastest erosion rates in Europe.

before.exam_tip_html: Eduqas examiner reports flag two recurring errors with hydrographs. First, students confuse peak rainfall with peak discharge — remember they happen at different times, separated by the lag. Second, students describe the graph but never explain it. For 6-mark questions, link a basin’s features (steep slopes, urban surfaces, deforested ground) to the shape of its hydrograph. Always name a UK case study (Calder Valley 2015, Cumbria 2009, Cornwall 2004) when asked about a specific flood.

For 8-mark evaluations on flood management, mark schemes reward you for weighing costs against benefits and reaching a clear judgement. Pick a real scheme (Carlisle, Belford, Calderdale) and use specific numbers (£38 million, 1,800 homes, 30 % peak reduction). Do not say soft engineering is ‘cheaper’ without explaining why. Examiners flag the misconception that hard engineering is always better — balanced answers show that the best schemes combine both, and that land-use zoning is what stops the next disaster.
before.content_html:
Two Approaches to the Same Problem

River flooding cannot be prevented forever, but the damage it does can be reduced. UK flood managers split their tools into two camps. Hard engineering works against the river, blocking, deepening or rerouting it with concrete and steel. Soft engineering works with the river, slowing water on the slopes above and giving it room to spread safely lower down. Most modern UK schemes combine the two.

Hard Engineering Options

Hard engineering is what flood defence used to mean. Dams hold floodwater back in reservoirs and release it gradually. Embankments and concrete walls raise the river banks so the channel holds more water. Channel straightening removes meanders to push water through faster. Demountable barriers slot into permanent foundations only when a flood is forecast.

Key Fact

Hard engineering protects high-value urban areas effectively, but it is expensive, can fail catastrophically if overtopped, and often shifts flooding downstream by sending water through faster.

Carlisle in Cumbria was overwhelmed in January 2005 when the Eden, Petteril and Caldew rivers all peaked at the same time. Three people died and around 1,800 homes flooded. After the disaster the Environment Agency built £38 million of new flood walls, raised embankments and demountable barriers along nearly 10 km of river. The scheme protected the city in storms that would once have flooded it — but extreme events such as Storm Desmond in 2015 still overtopped the defences in some streets, showing that hard engineering buys protection up to a design limit, not forever.

Soft Engineering Options

Soft engineering tries to give the river back some of the natural buffers human activity removed. Afforestation in upland catchments adds interception and slows runoff. Restoring meanders and reconnecting floodplains lets water spread out across grassland rather than racing through towns. Catchment-based management places small leaky dams of logs and brush in upland streams. River restoration programmes pull out concrete and re-meander straightened reaches.

A flagship UK example is the Belford Burn in Northumberland. Engineers built around 35 small woody dams across upland tributaries, plus ponds and wetlands, to hold up to 6,000 cubic metres of floodwater. The scheme cost less than £350,000 — far cheaper than a hard wall — and reduces peak flood levels in Belford village by an estimated 30 %. Such schemes also create habitat for fish, birds and insects.

Key Fact

Soft engineering is generally cheaper and more sustainable, creates wildlife habitat and works with natural processes — but it can rarely protect dense city centres on its own and needs years to take full effect.

Land-Use Zoning

Land-use zoning stops new flood damage by putting low-risk uses in high-risk places. The Environment Agency divides UK floodplains into Flood Zones 1 (lowest risk) to 3b (highest risk). New homes should not normally be built in Zone 3, while playing fields, car parks and parks are acceptable. The aim is that when the river does spill, it floods grass not bedrooms.

In practice, planning sometimes loses to political and economic pressure. Around 5 % of homes built in England since 2009 have been on Zone 3 floodplains. After every major flood, calls grow louder to enforce zoning more strictly.

Conflicting Views — The Future of UK Floodplains

Different groups want different futures for the same stretch of river. Property developers want cheap, flat land near towns — floodplains tick both boxes. Local councils need housing targets met. Insurance companies want flood risk reduced or premiums become unaffordable. Conservation groups want re-meandered rivers, beaver reintroductions and natural flood management. Farmers worry about new wetlands taking grazing out of production. Residents want their homes safe today — not flooded for the sake of someone’s future plan.

In a ‘hold the line’ future, government keeps building higher walls and bigger barriers around existing settlements. This protects historic city centres like York or Carlisle but costs more every decade as climate change pushes peaks higher. In a ‘give it room’ future, hard defences are kept around the highest-value areas but elsewhere rivers are allowed to spread across restored floodplains. Land use shifts: lowest-risk farms become wetland nature reserves, footpaths and meadows. The Calder catchment after 2015 has moved towards the second model, with millions invested in upland leaky dams and woodland.

Choosing the Right Mix

No single approach fits every river. Most UK schemes now blend a hard core of walls or barriers around towns with soft measures higher up the catchment. Land-use zoning prevents new damage. Climate-change projections add 20–50 % to design discharges. The fairest schemes consult residents, farmers and businesses before building — recognising that the future of every UK floodplain is also a social and political choice, not just an engineering one.
